title: The Diary
author: Alexandre Dias
contentWarnings: Themes of inherited responsibility and quiet reconciliation
excerpt: The diary was in the small cardboard box her mother had sent from Truro. Rebecca had, at ten, stopped writing in it. The last entry had been dated 12 August 1997. She turned the page. And the next. And the next. Then, twenty pages in, another entry appeared. In her own handwriting. Dated 8 March 2002.

chapters.title: Ink
chapters.body:
The diary was in the small cardboard box.

Rebecca Trethewey was thirty-seven, and she had, on a Sunday afternoon in November, been going through the small collection of boxes her mother had, that autumn, shipped to her from the small house in Truro where Rebecca had grown up. Her mother had, at seventy-one, sold the small house and had moved into a small flat in Falmouth, and had, in the specific small careful way of a widowed English mother arranging her small small final years, sent to each of her three children the small collection of small childhood things she had, throughout the last twenty-five years, kept in the small attic.

Rebecca had, that Sunday afternoon in her small flat in Bristol, opened the first of the boxes.

The box had contained a small assortment of small childhood objects — a small collection of small drawings from her primary school years, a small collection of small ceramic animals she had made in an art class at ten, a small pile of small letters her grandmother had, throughout Rebecca's childhood, written her from Penzance.

At the bottom of the box, in a small clear plastic bag, had been a small red diary.

Rebecca had, on seeing the small red diary, made a small small sound. She had taken it out of the small plastic bag. She had, in the small careful way of a woman recognizing an old object, held it in her hand.

The small diary had been a small red hardcover book with a small brass clasp at its right edge. It had been the specific small diary her mother had given her for her ninth birthday. It had had, on its small cover, in small embossed gold, the words *MY DIARY.* It had, throughout her ninth and tenth years, been the specific small book she had, in the specific small careful way of a small English girl of that period, written her small daily entries into.

She had, at eleven or twelve, stopped writing in it. She had, at that point, moved on to the small careful notebooks her mother had bought her at the small shop on Lemon Street. The small red diary had, from then on, sat on her small shelf as a small souvenir of her small childhood.

She had, at eighteen, when she had left for university, taken it with her.

She had, at twenty-three, when she had graduated and had begun her small first job in Bristol, still had it.

She had, at some small point in her mid-twenties — she could not, on quick reflection, remember exactly when — sent it back to her mother's house. She had, at that point in her life, been living in a small student flat with three flatmates and had been culling small unnecessary possessions, and the small diary, in the small honest way she had, at twenty-five or twenty-six, been being with herself, had felt like a small unnecessary childhood possession. She had, in the specific small careful way, packed it into a small parcel with several other small things and had sent them to her mother, on the theory that her mother would keep them in the small attic and that they would, at some future point in Rebecca's life, be available if she wanted them.

She had, until that Sunday afternoon in November, not thought about the small red diary in perhaps eleven years.

She had, sitting on the small carpet in her small sitting room with the small diary in her hand, opened it.

The small brass clasp had opened without ceremony.

The small pages had been the specific small pages she remembered. They had been small lined pages, printed with the specific small dates of the specific small year — 1996, the year of her ninth birthday, and the small first year of her diary. Each page had had, in her small careful ninth-year handwriting, a small daily entry.

She had, on the small first page — 1 January 1996 — smiled.

The small entry had read, in her small careful cursive: *Today I am nine. Mummy gave me this diary. I am going to write in it every day.*

She had, in the specific small pleasant way of a woman looking through her small childhood diary, turned the pages.

She had read a small entry from February. *Snowed today. Went sledding with Michael. He fell and cried.* She had read a small entry from June. *Sports day. Came third in the running race. Michael came first.* She had read a small entry from October. *Halloween. Dressed as a witch. Michael was a ghost.*

Michael had been her older brother. He had been eleven at the time. He had been, throughout her childhood, her small closest companion and her small greatest small tormentor.

He had died two years earlier, at forty-one, of pancreatic cancer.

Rebecca had, at the small entry for Halloween 1996, closed her eyes for a moment. She had, in the specific small careful way of a bereaved sister, permitted herself the specific small warm small pain of finding Michael in the small ordinary way. She had, at last, opened her eyes and had turned the small page.

She had, over the next hour, gone through the whole of 1996. She had gone through the small first months of 1997 — the small diary had, in the specific small way of many small childhood diaries, continued past its printed year, with Rebecca writing in the small blank pages at the small back of the small book. She had reached the small final entry.

The small final entry had been dated 12 August 1997. It had read: *Went to Grandma's for the summer. She is teaching me to bake bread. Tomorrow we will make butter.*

Rebecca had, on the small final entry, smiled.

She had turned the small page.

The next page had been blank. She had, in the specific small way, expected this. She had, at ten, stopped writing.

She had, in the small habitual way of a woman flipping through a small book, kept turning the pages.

The next page had also been blank.

The next.

The next.

She had, in the specific small careful way of a woman about to reach the small back cover of a small book she had, at ten, given up on, turned the next page.

The page had had, at the top, in her own small handwriting, a date and an entry.

The date had been *8 March 2002.*

The entry had read: *Started at the grammar school today. New uniform. Uniform is scratchy. Miss Bevis is the form mistress. She seems all right.*

Rebecca had, sitting on the small carpet, held the small diary very still.

She had, in the specific small careful way, considered the small entry.

She had considered that in March 2002 she had been fifteen. She had considered that she had, that year, indeed started at the small grammar school in Truro. She had considered that Miss Bevis had, indeed, been her form mistress that year. She had considered that the small uniform had, indeed, been scratchy.

She had considered, further, that she had not, at fifteen, been writing in the small red diary. At fifteen she had, in the specific small careful way, been writing in the small careful notebooks her mother had bought her at the small shop on Lemon Street. She had, at fifteen, considered the small red diary a small childhood object she had, in the specific small honest way of a small teenager, been embarrassed by.

She had not, so far as she remembered, ever added to it after August 1997.

But the small entry from 8 March 2002 was, unmistakably, in her handwriting. It was in the specific small careful handwriting of her fifteenth year — a small handwriting she recognized from the small careful notebooks, which she had kept, and which were, at that moment, in a small box in her small storage cupboard down the hall.

She had, in the specific small careful way, turned the page.

The next page had had, at the top, another entry.

The entry had been dated *14 March 2002.* It had read: *Miss Bevis kept me back after class today to ask if I was all right. I said I was fine. She said if I wasn't, I should tell someone. I do not know what she means. I am fine.*

Rebecca had, at the small entry, made a small small sound.

She had, in the specific small careful way, remembered this. She had remembered Miss Bevis. She had remembered the specific small conversation. She had remembered, in the small specific way of a woman who had, over the years, come to understand her fifteen-year-old self somewhat better than she had, at the time, understood herself, that Miss Bevis had been, in the small specific careful way of a woman who had seen many small careful teenagers, entirely correct in her small worry.

Rebecca had, at fifteen, not been fine. She had, at fifteen, been in the small careful early stages of the small careful eating disorder that had, over the following seven years, become the specific small careful defining feature of her small young adulthood.

She had, on remembering Miss Bevis, understood that the small entry was, in some specific small careful way, correct. She had, at fifteen, indeed said *I am fine* to Miss Bevis. She had, at fifteen, indeed not known what Miss Bevis meant. She had, at fifteen, indeed written the small entry.

But she had not written it in the small red diary.

The small red diary had, so far as she remembered, been at the bottom of her small chest of drawers in Truro that whole year, unopened and unthought-of.

She had, sitting on the small carpet in her small flat in Bristol on a Sunday afternoon in November at thirty-seven, turned the page again.

chapters.title: The Handwriting Growing Up
chapters.body:
The entries had continued.

They had continued, page by page, through the small remainder of what Rebecca had, on her nine-year-old assumption, taken to be the small blank pages of the diary. She had, over the following hour, sat on the small carpet and had read them slowly.

The entries had covered the whole of her fifteenth year. Small entries at intervals of perhaps two or three weeks. Small entries in the small handwriting of her fifteenth self. Small entries that had, on Rebecca's small careful reading, been entirely accurate — small careful records of small things that had, at fifteen, happened to her, and that she had, over the intervening twenty-two years, largely forgotten.

She had reached a small entry from December 2002 — *Christmas at Grandma's. I did not eat the pudding. Mummy noticed.* — and had, on that entry, felt the small careful chill of a specific small piece of evidence.

She had, at fifteen, indeed not eaten her grandmother's Christmas pudding. Her mother had, indeed, noticed. This had been, in the specific small careful way, the small specific moment at which her mother had, over the following weeks, first raised the small careful concern that had led, some months later, to the small careful referral to the small careful clinic in Truro and to the specific small careful start of the small careful treatment that had, over the following seven years, in the specific small careful way, saved her life.

Rebecca had, at the small December entry, understood that the small diary was recording her life.

Not — she had understood — recording it *after* the fact. Recording it, in some specific small careful way, *as it had happened.* Each small entry had been written in the small careful handwriting of Rebecca's fifteen-year-old self, using the small careful vocabulary and the small careful narrative economy of Rebecca at fifteen. Each small entry had been, in the specific small careful way, exactly the small entry Rebecca would have written if she had, at fifteen, been keeping the small diary.

She had, in the specific small careful way of a woman doing a small necessary check, turned to the next year. The entries had continued into 2003. Rebecca at sixteen. Rebecca in the specific small careful clinic. Rebecca at the small careful summer of 2003, at her grandmother's small house in Penzance, in the specific small careful way of a small careful sixteen-year-old learning to eat again. The handwriting, over those pages, had changed slightly. It had become, in the specific small careful way, the small handwriting of a slightly older girl. It had, on Rebecca's careful inspection, matched the specific small handwriting Rebecca had, throughout her sixteenth year, actually used.

She had turned to 2004. The handwriting had grown up further. She had turned to 2005. The handwriting had, on that year, become the small careful handwriting of Rebecca at eighteen — the specific small handwriting she had used in her small careful application to the university at Bristol.

She had turned to 2006. Rebecca at nineteen. Bristol. Her small careful first year. Small entries about her small careful lecture in the specific small careful way she had, at nineteen, written about her small careful lecture.

She had turned to 2007. Rebecca at twenty. Small entries about the specific small relationship she had, at twenty, had with a small careful classmate named Peter, who had, over the small careful following year, become in the specific small way her first small careful serious partner.

She had, in the specific small careful way, kept turning.

The small diary had had, at that small point in Rebecca's careful turning, a small number of pages remaining. Perhaps twenty. She had, at the small careful thought of the twenty remaining pages, understood something.

She had understood that the small diary had — in the specific small careful way of a small careful book — a specific small end. There were, in the small book, only so many pages. There were only so many entries the small diary could contain. And each entry, so far as she could tell in her small careful reading, was a specific small record of a specific small period of her small careful life.

She had, on quick calculation, understood that if the small diary continued to write itself at its current rate — an entry every two or three weeks, one page per entry — the small twenty remaining pages would cover, at most, the small careful next year of her life.

She had turned to the next entry.

It had been dated 15 December 2025.

She had, at the small entry, felt the small careful chill she had, on some part of her small careful mind, been expecting.

The entry had read:

*Told mother today. She asked if I was sure. I said I was.*

Rebecca had, at the small entry, looked up from the small diary.

She had, sitting on the small carpet in her small sitting room in Bristol on a Sunday afternoon in November of the current year, understood that the small entry was dated one month in the future.

She had, in the specific small careful way of a woman who had, over the last hour, been slowly accepting a small strange thing, understood that the small diary had, in the specific small careful way of a small careful book, arrived at its small careful present, and had begun, in the specific small careful way, to move slightly ahead.

She had, in the specific small careful way, turned the next page.

The next entry had been dated 3 January 2026.

*The pain has been worse this week. Dr. Wilkins says we need to run the scans again.*

Rebecca had, at the small entry, put the small diary down.

She had, in the specific small careful way, stood up. She had walked into her small kitchen. She had, at the small sink, poured herself a small glass of water. She had drunk it slowly.

She had, in the specific small careful way of a woman who had, at thirty-seven, been living with a small careful abdominal pain for the last six weeks that she had not, at any point, mentioned to anyone, understood two things.

She had understood, first, that the small diary was, in the specific small careful way, not fictional. It was recording her small careful life. It was, in the specific small careful way, going to go on recording her small careful life until it, in the specific small careful way, ran out of pages.

She had understood, second, that the small entry from 3 January 2026 suggested that whatever the small abdominal pain was, it was not, in the specific small careful way of the small ordinary muscular pain she had, on the last six weeks, been telling herself it was, going to resolve.

She had, at the small sink, poured herself a second small glass of water. She had drunk it slowly.

She had, at last, gone back to the small sitting room. She had sat back down on the small carpet. She had picked up the small diary.

She had, in the specific small careful way, turned the next page.

—

The entries had continued.

They had continued through the first several months of 2026. Small entries about Dr. Wilkins. Small entries about the small careful scans. Small entries about a small careful referral to a small careful specialist in London. Small entries — Rebecca had, at the small careful reading of them, sat very still — about a small careful diagnosis. Small entries about a small careful surgery. Small entries about a small careful recovery. Small entries about a small careful decision, in July of 2026, to leave her small careful job in Bristol and to move back to Truro, so as to be, in the specific small careful way, closer to her mother.

Rebecca had, at the small careful move-back-to-Truro entry, looked up.

She had understood, on looking up, that the small entries were suggesting a small careful future in which she had, in some specific small careful way, chosen to arrange the last small careful period of her life around her small careful mother.

She had understood, further, that the small entries were not saying, in any small careful way, that she was going to die.

She had, in the specific small careful way, kept reading.

The small entries had continued through the small careful autumn of 2026 and the small careful winter of 2026 and the small careful spring of 2027. Small entries about her small careful life in Truro. Small entries about her small careful mother, whose small careful health was, over the small careful spring, in the specific small careful way, declining. Small entries about the small careful April afternoon on which Rebecca had, in the specific small careful way, sat with her mother at the small careful end.

Rebecca had, at the small careful entry, closed the small diary.

She had, in the specific small careful way, understood.

She had understood that the small diary had, in the specific small careful way, not been written for her at any point in the last thirty years. It had been written *for her mother*.

She had understood, sitting on the small carpet in her small flat in Bristol on a Sunday afternoon in November, that the small diary was, in the specific small careful way of a small careful gift, a small careful summary of her small careful life prepared for the small careful moment at which her mother would, at some small careful point, need it.

Her mother had, at seventy-one, sent Rebecca the small careful box containing the small diary. Her mother had, so far as Rebecca could tell, not looked into the small diary. Her mother had, in the specific small careful way of a small careful English mother packing up a small careful attic, put the small childhood things into small careful boxes and had, in the specific small way, sent them without a small careful inspection.

But the small diary had, in the specific small careful way, been for her.

And her mother was going to, in the specific small careful way suggested by the small diary, need it — in the small specific careful way — sooner than Rebecca had, at any point in the last several months, been prepared to acknowledge.

Rebecca had, in the specific small careful way, understood that she was going to have to give it back.

chapters.title: The Last Pages
chapters.body:
She had, on the following morning, gone to Falmouth.

She had done this in the specific small careful way of a woman who had, over the small careful preceding evening, decided several things. She had, at eight in the morning, telephoned her small firm and had said that she needed to take a small careful personal day. She had, at nine, taken the small careful train from Bristol Temple Meads. She had, at just after one in the afternoon, arrived at her mother's small careful flat in Falmouth.

Her mother had, on her small careful arrival, been surprised.

She had said, at the small door: *Rebecca. My love. I was not expecting —*

Rebecca had said: *I know. Mother — may I come in.*

Her mother had, in the specific small careful way, let her in.

They had, in the small careful sitting room of the small careful flat, sat down. Her mother had, in the specific small way of an English mother, made a small pot of tea. They had sat with the small pot of tea.

Rebecca had, at the small careful moment, taken the small red diary out of her small careful bag.

She had said: *mother. I want to show you something.*

Her mother had, at the sight of the small red diary, made a small small sound.

Her mother had said: *your childhood diary. I put it in the box —*

Rebecca had said: *I know. Mother — I want you to look at it.*

Her mother had, in the specific small careful way, taken the small diary.

She had, at the small kitchen table, opened it.

She had, over the following twenty minutes, read the small diary slowly.

Rebecca had, over those twenty minutes, watched her mother's small careful face.

Her mother's face had, over the small careful minutes, done several things. It had, over the first small careful minutes, been the specific small warm face of a mother reading her small careful daughter's small childhood diary. It had, at some small careful point in the following minutes, become the specific small careful face of a mother who was understanding, in the specific small careful way, that the small diary was, in the specific small way, doing something the small careful ordinary diaries of small ordinary daughters did not do. It had, at the small careful point at which the small diary had reached March 2002, become the specific small careful face of a woman who had, in the specific small careful way, understood the small careful thing.

Her mother had, at the small entry for December 2002, made a small small sound.

Her mother had, at the small careful entry for the pain becoming worse in January 2026, made a small other sound.

Her mother had, at the small careful entry for the move back to Truro, put down the small careful diary and had, in the specific small careful way, looked at her small careful daughter.

Her mother had said: *Rebecca.*

Rebecca had said: *yes, mother.*

Her mother had said: *when — when is the pain.*

Rebecca had said: *six weeks. I have not — I have not told anyone.*

Her mother had said: *and Dr. Wilkins.*

Rebecca had said: *I have an appointment for next week. I made it — I made it this morning, before I came to see you.*

Her mother had said, in the specific small careful voice: *good.*

Her mother had, in the specific small careful way, closed the small diary.

She had, at the small careful table, held it in her small careful hands for a long moment.

She had said, at last, quietly: *do you know why it has come.*

Rebecca had said: *no.*

Her mother had said: *my mother had one.*

Rebecca had, at this, been quiet.

Her mother had said: *I did not — I did not know it. Not until she died. She left it to me in the small careful box with her other small careful things. I found it. I did not, at the small careful time, understand what I was looking at. But I read it, in the small careful weeks after she died. I read it and I understood.*

*It had been her small careful summary. Prepared, in the specific small careful way, for me. So that when she was gone, I would have a small careful record of the whole of her life. Not the whole of the small ordinary parts. The whole of the small important parts. The small parts that a mother wants her small careful daughter to know.*

*It had been, in the specific small careful way, a small final gift.*

Rebecca had said, quietly: *and yours.*

Her mother had, at this, been quiet.

Her mother had said, at last: *I have not — I have not yet found mine. I have thought about it. I have wondered, in the last several years, whether one is being prepared for me. I do not know. I have not — I have not, in the specific small careful way, looked.*

Rebecca had said: *mother.*

Her mother had said: *what.*

Rebecca had said: *when — when we clear out your things. In whatever small careful year. If we find one — if we find yours —*

Her mother had said, quietly: *I would like you to read it.*

Rebecca had said: *yes.*

Her mother had said: *I would like you to read the whole of it. I have not — I have not been the small easy mother I could have been. I have not been, in the small ordinary way, entirely clear. I would like — I would like the small diary to be, in the specific small careful way, the small careful record you could have made of me if I had, at any point, been able to explain myself.*

Rebecca had said: *mother, you have explained yourself.*

Her mother had said, quietly: *not enough.*

They had, at the small careful table, sat with the small careful tea.

—

Rebecca had, in the specific small careful way suggested by the small diary, arranged her small careful life.

She had, on the small careful Tuesday, seen Dr. Wilkins. Dr. Wilkins had, in the specific small careful way of a small careful GP in Bristol, ordered the small careful scans. The small careful scans had, in the specific small careful way, shown the small careful thing. The small careful specialist in London had, in the specific small careful way, confirmed the small careful diagnosis. The small careful surgery had, in the specific small careful way, happened in July.

Rebecca had, in the specific small careful way, recovered.

She had, in the specific small careful way, resigned from her small careful job in Bristol. She had, in the specific small careful way, moved back to Truro. She had, in the specific small careful way, taken up a small careful part-time consulting position with a small careful firm in Truro that specialized in the specific small careful work she had, in Bristol, been doing.

She had, in the specific small careful way, spent the whole of the small careful autumn and winter of 2026 with her small careful mother.

Her mother had, over that small careful autumn and winter, in the specific small careful way, declined.

Rebecca had, throughout the small careful decline, been with her.

They had, over those small careful months, talked. They had talked, in the small careful way of a mother and daughter who had, at last, been permitted the small careful time, about a great many small careful things. They had talked about Rebecca's small careful childhood. They had talked about Rebecca's small careful eating disorder, which had, in the small careful way of certain small careful painful subjects, been the small careful subject the two of them had, throughout Rebecca's twenties and thirties, most carefully avoided. They had talked about Rebecca's small careful father, who had died when Rebecca had been twenty-eight, and about whom her mother had, in the small careful way of certain small careful English widows, throughout the last nine years, said very little. They had talked about Michael, who had died two years earlier, and about whom the two of them had, in the small careful way of a mother and a sister sharing a specific small careful grief, been unable to speak until the small careful autumn of 2026.

Rebecca had, over those months, come to understand her small careful mother in the specific small careful way she had not, in her small careful life, understood her before.

She had understood, in that small careful understanding, that her mother had — in the specific small careful way of certain small careful English mothers — loved her deeply, and had not, in the specific small careful way, been able to show it, and had, over the last many years, been quietly aware of this, and had, in the small careful autumn of her small careful life, been given the small careful chance to correct it.

Rebecca had, in the specific small careful way, received the correction.

Her mother had, on a small careful afternoon in April 2027, quietly died.

Rebecca had been with her.

—

Rebecca had, in the specific small careful way, gone through her mother's things.

She had done this over the following weeks, in the small careful quiet way of a bereaved daughter. She had gone through the small careful clothes. She had gone through the small careful books. She had gone through the small careful letters and the small careful photographs and the small careful small things.

She had, in the specific small careful way, been looking for the small careful diary.

She had, at last, found it.

It had been in the small careful bottom drawer of her mother's small careful bedside table. It had been in a small careful cardboard box. It had been a small careful hardcover book with a small careful brass clasp — the small careful diary her mother had, at nine, been given by *her* mother, in the specific small careful family way.

Rebecca had, at the small careful bottom drawer, taken it out.

She had, in the specific small careful way, sat on her mother's small careful bed.

She had opened the small careful diary.

She had, over the following several evenings, read it.

She had read it slowly. She had read it in the specific small careful way her mother had, on that small careful afternoon in November of the previous year, asked her to. She had read the whole of it — the whole of the small careful early entries in her mother's small careful childhood handwriting, the small careful entries of the small careful adolescence, the small careful entries of the small careful young adulthood.

She had read the small careful entries about her father.

She had read the small careful entries about the small careful decision, in 1982, to have a small careful first child, who had been Michael.

She had read the small careful entries about the small careful second pregnancy, in 1986, which had, in the specific small careful way, been Rebecca.

She had, in the specific small careful way, come to know her mother in a way she had not, at any point in her small careful life, known her before.

—

She had, over the small careful years that followed, kept both diaries.

She had kept them together in a small careful box in the small careful drawer of her own small careful bedside table. She had, over the years, occasionally taken them out and had read a small careful entry or two.

She had, at fifty-two, understood that she was, in the specific small careful way, going to have to think about the small careful next one.

She had done this in the specific small careful way. She had, in her small careful spare time, at the small careful weekends, sat at a small careful desk and had, in the specific small careful way, begun to write.

She had written, in her small careful hand, a small careful diary for the small careful daughter she had not had.

She had, in the specific small careful way, made small careful entries. Small entries at intervals of perhaps two or three weeks. Small entries in her small careful handwriting. Small entries that had, in the specific small careful way, covered the small careful facts of her small careful life.

She had, at some small careful point in her small careful sixties, understood that she was, in the specific small careful way, writing the small careful diary for no one.

She had not, in the specific small careful way, had a small careful daughter. She had not, in her small careful life, been able to. She had, in the small careful way of a small careful woman who had come to accept this, been at peace with it. But she had, in the specific small careful way, understood that the small careful diary was, in her small careful case, not going to be read.

She had, at sixty-eight, considered whether to keep writing.

She had, in the specific small careful way, decided to keep writing.

She had decided this because she had, over the years, come to understand that the small careful diary was, in some specific small careful way, not entirely for the small careful reader. It was, in some specific small careful way, for the small careful writer. It was, in the specific small careful way, the small careful thing a small careful woman did when she had, in the specific small careful way, been given a small careful family diary and had, in the specific small careful way, understood that she was, at some small careful point, going to be one of the small careful writers.

She had, in the specific small careful way, kept writing.

She had died at eighty-one, of a small careful stroke, in the specific small careful way, in her small careful flat in Truro.

The small careful executor of her small careful estate — a small careful niece she had, over the small careful years, come to be close to — had, in the small careful clearing-out of her small careful things, found the small careful box in the small careful bedside drawer.

The small careful box had contained three small careful diaries. Two small hardcover books with small brass clasps — one small red, one small blue. And a third, larger, more recent, in a small careful modern hardcover notebook of the specific small careful sort Rebecca had, in her small careful sixties, taken to buying at a small careful shop in Truro.

The small careful niece had, in the specific small careful way, read them.

She had, in the specific small careful way, understood.

She had, in her small careful thirties, understood that she was, in some small careful way, next.

She had, in her own small careful way, begun to write.

The small careful family, so far as anyone knows, has been writing since 1902, when the specific small careful first diary was, in some specific small careful way, given by a small careful grandmother to a small careful granddaughter in a small careful house in west Cornwall.

The specific small careful writing has, in the specific small careful way, gone on.

It is, so far as anyone knows, still going on.
